source_refs.note: Topic 21.4 with Quick Check 21.3, answered (PDF 82-84); equations are condensed and the amine series and silver nitrate test redrawn. The quaternary salt is named tetraethylammonium bromide. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Hydroxide ion is both a good nucleophile and a good base, so a halogenoalkane can give substitution or elimination products, depending on the conditions. The reactions are done at higher temperature under reflux, to avoid losing volatile products. Bromoethane gives ethanol with aqueous sodium hydroxide and ethene with sodium hydroxide in ethanol:

blocks.alt: Bromoethane, CH3CH2Br, in the centre with five arrows. With NaOH(aq) and heat it gives ethanol, CH3CH2OH + NaBr (substitution). With NaOH in ethanol and heat it gives ethene, CH2=CH2 + H2O + NaBr (elimination). With KCN in ethanol under reflux it gives propanenitrile, CH3CH2CN + KBr (substitution). With NH3 in ethanol, heat and pressure it gives ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2 + HBr (substitution). With AgNO3 in water and ethanol, Br- + Ag+ gives a cream precipitate of AgBr, which shows bromine.
blocks.caption: Reactions of bromoethane (original diagram after the book's displayed equations).
blocks.long_description: Hydroxide ions act as a nucleophile in water and give the alcohol, but as a base in ethanol and give the alkene. Cyanide ions and ammonia are nucleophiles: cyanide adds one carbon to the chain (a nitrile), ammonia gives an amine. Silver nitrate does not change the carbon chain; the cream silver bromide precipitate is a test for the bromine in the compound.

items: Elimination (in ethanol): CH3CH2Br + NaOH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O + NaBr

blocks.text: The cyanide ion is a strong nucleophile but a weak base, so it gives substitution: a nitrile. The halogenoalkane is heated under reflux with potassium cyanide in ethanol. Bromoethane gives propanenitrile: CH3CH2Br + KCN -> CH3CH2CN + KBr.

Ammonia is a good nucleophile and reacts with halogenoalkanes heated in ethanol under pressure: C2H5Br + NH3 -> C2H5NH2 (ethylamine, ethanamine) + HBr. The amine formed is itself a nucleophile and competes with ammonia, so further substitution gives N-ethylethanamine, (C2H5)2NH, then N,N-diethylethanamine, (C2H5)3N. With a large excess of bromoethane the final product is the quaternary ammonium salt, tetraethylammonium bromide, (C2H5)4N+ Br-. Different amines can be obtained by carefully controlling the amounts used.

blocks.alt: A staircase of boxes: NH3 (ammonia), C2H5NH2 (ethanamine, primary amine), (C2H5)2NH (N-ethylethanamine, secondary), (C2H5)3N (N,N-diethylethanamine, tertiary) and (C2H5)4N+ Br- (tetraethylammonium bromide, a quaternary salt), each step labelled + C2H5Br.
blocks.caption: Successive substitution of ammonia by bromoethane (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: Each amine still has a lone pair on nitrogen, so it can attack another bromoethane molecule. One ethyl group is added at each step until the nitrogen carries four ethyl groups and a positive charge.

blocks.text: The reaction is done in a mixture of water and ethanol; the ethanol helps the halogenoalkane dissolve. Water acts as a nucleophile and replaces the halogen: CH3CH2X + H2O -> CH3CH2OH + H+ + X-. The halide ion released then reacts with silver nitrate to give a precipitate whose colour shows which halogen was present.
